messages.subject: Announcement: Second edition of QCLWR
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

Just a quick announcement that I have now finally submitted the manuscript for the second edition of QCLWR to the publisher. It features

- 243 single-spaced pages (i.e., it's probably about 10% longer than the first edition);
- nearly 7000 lines of now extremely heavily commented code: just about every code line is commented now and longer function calls are usually broken up so as to comment every single argument, like this (from one script):

############################################################
current.words <- exact.matches.2( # make current.words what you get when looking for
   "(?<={)[^\n\\{\\}]+(?=\\}\n)", # anything with a { to its left, not curly brackets and linebreaks in it, and a } before \n to its right
   current.sentences,             # in current.sentences
   gen.conc.output=FALSE)[1:2]    # don't generate concordances and retain both the matches and their (sentence) locations

current.sentences <- tapply( # make current sentences the result of applying to
   current.words[[1]],       # the matches (i.e., the words)
   current.words[[2]],       # a grouping by their locations (in the sentences)
   paste, collapse=" ")      # and then paste the grouped words together with spaces

[...]

# excursus 3: add the logic of excursus 1 to that of excursus 2 and this is what could be all that's done in the loop,
# i.e., this could replace all of lines 20-41 (leaves empty character strings in, but otherwise identical)
i                                                        %>%
scan(what=character(), sep="\n", quiet=TRUE)             %>%
paste(collapse="\n")                                     %>%
strsplit("<sent>")                                       %>%
unlist                                                   %>%
"["(-1)                                                  %>%
exact.matches.2("(?<={)[^}]+", .,
                gen.conc.output=FALSE, vectorize=FALSE)  %>%
"[["(1)                                                  %>%
sapply(paste, collapse=" ")                              %>%
cat(file=paste0(
   "../_outputfiles/05_18_icegb-output/",
   basename(i)), sep="\n")
############################################################

- many small changes and tweaks that arose from multiple years of bootcamp/workshop teaching (e.g., some small exercises tested in bootcamps, the use of free-spacing, etc., and many other small things);
- a revised section on programming times and a new section on writing your own functions (like SFLWR2, but of course with an emphasis on text processing);
- a revised section on Unicode;
- a new section on XML-processing using the packages XML and xml2;
- a slightly wider range of corpora being used than the first edition (now with a focus on XML rather than SGML);
- a new chapter 5 with 30+ case study assignments (some from the assignments of the first edition, but many new and all revised) on dispersion, frequency lists and key words, co-occurrence data, and other applications; new tweaks include code alternatives with dplyr's %>%, several applications of how to write and use useful functions for corpus processing, a new extended version of exact.matches, the use of conditional expression to have scripts use different search expressions or the right packages on different OS's, etc.); with very few exceptions, all case studies have the following four-part structure (this is quoted from the book):
What are the things we will need to do?: This section explains in plain English which steps the relevant task involves; it uses hardly any R code but already introduces the kinds and names of a few data structures that the script will contain;
What are the functions we will need for that?: This section lists all the main functions one will need to use to perform the things implied by the description formulated in the previous step;
Thus, this is the overall structure of the script: This section provides a skeleton of the R code we will use in what is called pseudocode: a description of the algorithm and structure of a program that performs a particular task; it is imperative that you read this part with the relevant script open in RStudio because in the pseudocode I will provide the line numbers of the relevant R script from the companion website so you can see exactly which lines of code in the script do which part of the pseudocode, or how the pseudocode is 'translated' into actual R code. The files with all the scripts are in the folder <_qclwr2/_scripts/> and all being with "05_"; this part will greatly help you understand the logic of the scripts;
Which aspects of the script are worth additional comment?: If you look at the script files, you will see that they are very heavily commented: often even a single function call is broken up into several lines so that each argument can be explained, and sometimes I will break down regular expressions into multiple lines (remember free-spacing from above?) to explain everything in detail. However, sometimes scripts involve something that I think merits additional explanation here, or they involve something you haven't seen yet at all or in the form in which something is used. If there are such situations – and not every case study has such parts – then this section provides additional discussion of these aspects of the scripts.
- plus, as soon as I have been resuscitated, I will be working on again providing some additional assignments for the companion website;
- the book uses pretty much only freely-available corpora, for users who don't have the few corpora that are not freely available, it provides additional assignments that change a freely available corpus into the exact format of the non-freely available one so they can then work as if they had that other corpus. (You definitely should have/get the BNC XML tho.)

Apologies for the self-promotion, but I thought this might be of interest to at least some of you. If it is, don't forget to buy hardcover copies for yourself and all your friends and family ;-) The current planned publication is, unfortunately, only 2 Dec 2016, but I will do my best with speedy proof corrections etc. to make things go as fast as possible.

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
----------------------------------
Univ. of California, Santa Barbara
http://tinyurl.com/stgries
